coach_says: You're a piece down, so you need forcing play, and your doubled rooks on the g-file are your best asset: g2 is attacked twice and only the queen and king defend it. Rxg2+ Qxg2 Rxg2+ Kxg2 gives up both rooks for the queen and a pawn, and then Qg6+ starts a string of checks against the bare king that White can't escape easily, so you're back to roughly level. Qe6 was too slow: after g3 the g-file is shut and you're simply a piece down. When you're losing, look first at the checks and captures your stacked pieces allow.
concept: break through on g2 with the doubled rooks

coach_says: Your e4 pawn was attacked by the knight on f6 and nothing defended it, and Kh1 did nothing about that, so Black simply took it with Nxe4. Before a quiet move like Kh1, ask what your opponent is attacking. d3 was the natural fix: it defends e4 and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop at the same time.
concept: left the e4 pawn undefended

coach_says: 1...e5 is the Englund Gambit: Black is offering you the e5 pawn. dxe5 takes it, and Black has nothing real for it. After Nf3 Black can play ...e4 instead and kick your knight, and the extra pawn is gone. When an opponent offers a centre pawn early and you can't see a trap, take it.
concept: accept the gambit pawn

coach_says: Black's king is on e7 with only your e4 knight in between, so a rook on the e-file sets up discovered checks. After Rfe1 you threaten Ng3+, uncovering check from the rook while the knight attacks the f5 bishop, so Black has to spend a move getting the king off the file. Bd3 let Black play Ne5 with tempo on your bishop and you lost that pressure. When the enemy king sits on an open file behind one of your pieces, put a rook behind it.
concept: rook behind the knight for discovered check
also: open file against an uncastled king

coach_says: White's bishop on d5 is their best piece, and Ne5 would have hit the queen on f3 and then let you play Bxd5 to trade it off. Bc8 took a developed bishop backwards, left your king stuck in the centre, and handed White free time to bring the rest of their pieces in. Look for moves that attack something (here the queen) while improving a piece, and trade off your opponent's strongest piece when you can.
concept: kick the queen, trade the strong bishop
also: undeveloping move with the king in the centre

coach_says: Rxa8 was the best move: taking the rook back is the most you can get out of a tough position. Keep going and stay active with what you have.
concept: none

coach_says: Castling here was as good as d4 or Nc3: get the king safe, then develop and use the open e-file against Black's queen. Fine move.
concept: none

coach_says: Retreating the bishop to c8 is about as good as Bd7 or Be6: it was attacked by the knight on e3 and you kept it. You're an exchange up, so calm moves like this are fine.
concept: none

coach_says: Kf8 gets out of check sensibly and you're still clearly better. Re6 to block and fight for the e-file was slightly stronger, but the difference is small.
concept: none
also: block with a rook to contest the file

coach_says: Re1 lines up a discovered attack on the queen behind your e2 bishop, but Black simply castles and the threat is gone. Nc3 was better: it develops a piece and attacks the queen straight away, so you gain time to make up for the pawn you gave. When you're a pawn down in the opening, prefer moves that develop and hit something at once.
concept: develop with tempo on the queen

coach_says: Your e6 pawn was attacked by the d4 knight and nothing defended it, and Nxe6 would land with a fork of your queen and rook. Rad8 didn't fix that, and after Nxe6 Rxd1 Nxc5 you lose the pawn and soon b7 too. Qb6 would have guarded e6 along the sixth rank. Before each move, check which of your pawns are loose and what lands on that square if they're taken.
concept: loose e6 pawn and knight fork

coach_says: White's d4 bishop was staring at your a7 bishop and the g7 pawn, threatening Bxa7 Rxa7 Qd4 to hit the rook and g7 together. Bxd4 to trade first, or Nf6 to block the long diagonal, dealt with it. b5 ignored the threat and also opened the diagonal from d5 to a8, so Bd5 attacked your rook as well. When an enemy piece faces one of yours, trade or defend before starting pawn moves on the wing.
concept: ignored the double threat on the diagonals

coach_says: White's bishop on h4 had no defender, and Qh6 attacks it while lining your queen up with the g4 knight against h2. White has to play Bg3, the only retreat that still covers h2, and then ...f5 and ...f4 keep the pressure on. Be6 was a quiet move that let White play b4 with tempo on your c5 bishop and take over. When you see an undefended enemy piece, look for a move that attacks it and something else.
concept: attack the undefended h4 bishop

coach_says: Your d4 knight was attacked twice, but Nxe6 answered that by attacking first: the knight takes a free pawn and forks the queen on c5 and both rooks. After Nxe6 Rxd1 Nxc5 Rxf1+ Rxf1 you are two pawns up with the b7 pawn falling too. c3 defended the knight but missed the chance. When one of your pieces is under attack, check whether it can move with a bigger threat of its own.
concept: missed the knight fork on e6

coach_says: Taking back with the c-pawn was best: cxd5 undoubles your c-pawns, gives you a strong pawn centre and keeps the f6 knight guarding your king. After Nxd5 White just plays Qxe5, winning the e5 pawn while hitting your e7 bishop and d5 knight, and you are still left with weak doubled c-pawns. When you have doubled pawns, a capture with the pawn that fixes them is often the natural recapture.
concept: recapture with the pawn toward the centre

coach_says: Your d4 pawn was held by c3 and the f3 knight against Black's c6 knight and g7 bishop. c4 took away the pawn support, and after ...g4 the knight has to move, so d4 simply falls. Bb5 was better, pressuring the c6 knight that attacks d4. Before you move a pawn that defends another, count the attackers and defenders again, and watch for pawns that can kick your remaining defender.
concept: removed the pawn support of d4

coach_says: e3 was the move: the pawn attacks your opponent's rook on f2, so it advances with tempo and becomes a dangerous passed pawn only two squares from queening. If the rook goes to f3, Bc6 attacks it down the newly opened diagonal and wins the exchange. Qd5 was a decent square for the queen but let White blockade the pawn. When you have an advanced passed pawn, look for a push that hits something.
concept: push the passed pawn with tempo
also: Bc6 wins the exchange on f3

coach_says: Kb5 put your king where a white pawn on c4 would attack it together with d5. White answers Rxd5+ Rxd5 c4+, forking king and rook, and the pawn ending that follows is lost. Rf6 or Kc5 kept things level. In rook endings, before moving your king near enemy pawns, check whether a rook trade followed by a pawn fork is possible.
concept: walked into a pawn fork
also: trade into a lost pawn ending

coach_says: Your e4 pawn was attacked twice (knight f6, rook e8) and defended only by the c3 knight. Rfe1 added a defender, but Black replies b4, chasing the knight away, and you have to trade it off on d5. f3 defends e4 with a pawn, which can't be chased, and keeps your knight for the d5 square. When defending a pawn, a pawn defender is usually more reliable than a piece the opponent can kick.
concept: defend e4 with a pawn, not a piece

coach_says: h3 is a perfectly good move, asking the bishop question and giving your king air. Bxc6 was slightly more precise, but the difference is tiny.
concept: none
